correctness.rationale: Stationarity against arbitrary antiderivatives of the voltage coordinate gives \(\mathbb E[w\mid v]=F(v)\), and arbitrary antiderivatives of the recovery coordinate give \(\mathbb E[v\mid w]=bw-a\). The two residuals are exactly \(-\dot v\) and \(\dot w/\varepsilon\), so the law of total variance yields both speed defects and their sum. If either squared-speed expectation vanishes, continuity plus invariance of the support forces both coordinates to be constant along every support trajectory, hence the support lies in the equilibrium set. For every non-equilibrium-supported invariant measure, each speed has mean zero and nonzero second moment, so each takes both signs on positive-measure sets. The packaged checker independently confirms the polynomial residual identities, equilibrium polynomial, and standard-parameter coefficients.

originality.rationale: The complete 2003 public preprint later published as the 2004 bifurcation paper was inspected and contains the equivalent cubic planar system, global boundedness, Lyapunov analysis, equilibria, and rich periodic/homoclinic bifurcations; targeted full-text searches found no average, moment, invariant-measure, or conditional formulation. A recent full article that specifically studies FitzHugh–Nagumo time averages was inspected because it is the strongest thematic coverage found; it analyzes approximate parameter insensitivity of the slow-variable cycle average, not exact conditional means at fixed parameters. Direct semantic-index and web searches over nullcline, conditional-regression, variance-defect, and mean-square-speed aliases found no same-object statement implying the accepted theorem. The originality claim is restricted to the two universal conditional nullcline regressions, the exact speed-defect identities, equality rigidity, and the stationary two-sided nullcline consequence.

value.rationale: The cubic voltage nullcline and linear recovery nullcline are the organizing objects of FitzHugh–Nagumo excitability, while modern work continues to interpret long-run averages of the fast and slow variables. The accepted theorem connects those two viewpoints exactly: each nullcline is a stationary conditional regression, and the two deviations from the nullclines are measured by the mean-square coordinate speeds. The resulting Pythagorean variance budget distinguishes equilibrium mixtures from every genuinely time-dependent stationary state and forces such states to occupy both sides of both nullclines. This gives a parameter-explicit, simulation-checkable structural diagnostic for periodic or stationary data and a mathematically natural refinement of phase-plane nullcline geometry rather than a routine recomputation of an equilibrium or local bifurcation.
